extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory; policymakers and commentators on democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate how the unbounded power of a majority in democratic republics affects law, administration, opinion, and character; and what institutional or social features mitigate or aggravate that power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between tyranny and arbitrary power
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction must be drawn between tyranny and arbitrary power: 'Tyranny may be exercised by means of the law, and in that case it is not arbitrary; arbitrary power may be exercised for the good of the community at large, in which case it is not tyrannical.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this conceptual separation when assessing abuses: tyranny = legal/oppressive rule via law; arbitrary power = extralegal acts possibly intended for public good. Recognize that tyranny often uses arbitrary means but can exist without them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority control over lawmaking and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority has an entire control over the law when it is made and when it is executed; it possesses equal authority over those who are in power and the community at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutions by whether the majority can both create laws and direct their execution (centralized authority). Where both powers are concentrated, risk of despotism increases. Look for signs that public officers act as passive agents of the majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public officers treated as agents of the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority considers public officers as its passive agents and readily confides the task of serving its designs to their vigilance; details of office and privileges are rarely defined beforehand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether office-holders have well-defined, protected spheres of action. If magistrates are constantly directed or reprimanded by majority sentiment, administrative independence is weak and arbitrary implementation likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral power of the majority upon opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: When the majority has once irrevocably decided a question, all discussion ceases; the majority possesses a power which is physical and moral at the same time, acting upon the will as well as the actions of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the social pressure to conform: if public debate shuts down after a majority decision and dissenters face ostracism, freedom of opinion is effectively curtailed even without legal sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social sanctions and ostracism as instruments of despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of physical coercion, democratic despotism often uses exclusion, slights, persecutions, denial of advancement, and daily obloquy to punish dissent ('You will remain among men, but you will be deprived of the rights of mankind').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating civic freedom, account for informal penalties (career death, social shunning). These may be more effective and less visible than legal punishment; assess their prevalence and impact on public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of literary and intellectual freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no literary genius without freedom of opinion; the empire of the majority 'removes the wish' to publish controversial works—authors self-censor because the majority's decency and order make such works unpopular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging national intellectual life, examine whether writers and thinkers refrain from publishing or organizing because of social consequences, not only legal bans. The absence of public organs for certain opinions (e.g., infidelity) signals social, not just legal, suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on national character and leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The tyranny of the majority checks the development of leading characters, extends the practice of currying favor with the many, and debases citizens' characters by encouraging servility and loss of independent judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political culture for prevalence of sycophancy, careerism, and conformity. A system that rewards flattery and penalizes independence will produce fewer distinguished, independent leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk that majority's misuse of power produces anarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic republics are more likely to perish from a misuse of their power than by impotence; the unlimited authority of the majority may drive minorities to desperation and physical force, producing anarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether institutional safeguards prevent majority excesses that could provoke violent backlash. Consider how concentrated, energetic democratic power might, through abuse, undermine social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party-dominated exclusion from public employment
rubrics_metrics.description: The author (and editor's note) describes a system where the 'tyranny of the party' excludes from public employment those who do not adopt the Shibboleth of the majority, extending to low-level offices and enforced by electors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating civil service fairness, examine patronage and partisan purges. Exclusion of opponents from office for political beliefs is a measurable manifestation of majority/party tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of judiciary independence as a check
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary's independence and its means of controlling the action of a majority are critical; the jury is not the whole judicial power, and an independent bench can afford redress for wrongs committed by the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess separation of powers: an independent judiciary with real review powers mitigates majority despotism. Check for institutional features (lifetime tenure, impartial appointment processes, review jurisdiction) that protect judicial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary majorities vs permanent domination
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority of yesterday may become the minority of to-day; frequent changes of popular sentiment can reverse injustices, so temporary preponderance should not be conflated with permanent despotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between transient political dominance and structural, enduring domination. Look for evidence of reversibility of partisan exclusions or whether injustices persist across cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of centralized administration as mitigating tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Although governments in the United States are centralized in power, centralized administration is nearly unknown; the national majority does not conduct all business and must employ town and county magistrates to execute decisions, which mitigates tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate decentralization of administration: dispersal of executional authority to local magistrates and defined administrative boundaries reduces the majority's capacity to micromanage and repress. Identify whether administrative fragmentation limits majority control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil vs moral instruments of coercion in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic republics have refined the arts of despotism: fetters and headsmen are replaced by moral and social instruments that enslave the soul while leaving the body free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing authoritarian risk, include non-physical coercion: propaganda, social ostracism, control of honors and careers. These subtler instruments can achieve conformity without overt repression.
